case_study_insert.main_stem: Eastline Power (ELP) is a public limited company in the electricity generation and supply sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 2008 by Amina Yusuf, it supplies electricity to households and small businesses and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. ELP plans to invest $1,200,000 in a smart-meter rollout and battery storage units, financed by a $700,000 share issue and a $500,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $1,500,000 a year, a variable cost of $60 a unit and a selling price of $85, and currently supplies 150,000 units a year. ELP faces a service problem: billing complaints have reached 6.1% of customers and skilled-engineer turnover is rising, while its network reports increasing outage hours.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Customer Service and Network Report — Q3 2025: ELP served 38,000 accounts last quarter with a billing-complaint rate of 6.1%, up from 3.8% a year ago. Complaints rose from 92 to 168 per month. Average outage duration is 3.4 hours per customer and the network fault rate is 2.9%. Meter-reading accuracy is 96.5%. A skills review shows 30 of 120 engineers have not completed on-the-job training on the new smart meters; off-the-job training at the technical institute is also under consideration. HR is considering formal appraisals and a performance-related bonus to cut engineer turnover.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Eastline Power for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.5%, increasing borrowing costs for capital-intensive utilities. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $12.40 to $13.50 an hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across the energy sector. (3) Wholesale gas and carbon-permit input costs have risen 14.2% year-on-year, energy inflation is 9.8%, and household electricity demand grew 2.7%.

questions.question_text: ELP plans to fund part of its $1,200,000 smart-meter programme with a $700,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for ELP of using a share issue instead of the $500,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $700,000 share issue raises equity that needs no interest or repayment, protecting cash flow while ELP already carries fixed costs of $1,500,000 a year and a $500,000 bank loan. With the base rate rising to 5.5% (Appendix 3), debt would cost more, so equity keeps the smart-meter rollout affordable and leaves more cash to cut the 6.1% billing-complaint rate and the 3.4-hour outages.

Point 2: Equity improves ELP's financial resilience because there is no risk of the $1,200,000 programme being jeopardised by loan covenants or repossession if demand grows only 2.7%. As a public limited company, ELP can access a wide pool of investors, spreading the funding risk among many shareholders rather than one lender, and the new capital supports the battery storage units without forcing Amina Yusuf to rely solely on retained profits or further borrowing.

Equity also avoids adding to the interest burden on the $500,000 bank loan at a time when the base rate has risen from 4.75% to 5.5%, protecting the $1,200,000 programme from debt-service pressure.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to ELP and the case data.

questions.question_text: ELP is promoting its new smart-meter rollout. Consider national television advertising, door-to-door sales teams, or social media campaigns. Which should ELP choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: TV could quickly inform millions of households about smart meters and help justify the $1,200,000 programme, but airtime is costly for a utility whose fixed costs are already $1,500,000 a year, and it cannot answer individual questions about the 6.1% billing complaints or 3.4-hour outages. Much of the audience is outside ELP's supply area, so spend would be wasted.

Door-to-door sales teams: Trained staff can explain smart meters face to face, verify meter reading accuracy of 96.5% and immediately address the 168 monthly complaints, rebuilding trust where the complaint rate has risen from 3.8% to 6.1%. This is highly targeted to ELP's 38,000 accounts. The drawbacks are high labour costs when the minimum wage rises 6.0%, slow coverage of a large customer base and variable quality across 120 engineers.

Social media campaigns: Low-cost, targeted ads can reach households and small businesses with installation dates and energy-saving advice, and are easy to update. However, they lack the personal reassurance many customers need after 3.4-hour outages and depend on customers actively engaging with the message.

Recommendation: ELP should choose door-to-door sales teams. Given that 6.1% of customers already complain and the network fault rate is 2.9%, direct contact restores confidence and supports the $700,000 share-issue-funded rollout far better than mass media. Television is rejected as expensive and untargeted, and social media is rejected as too impersonal for a service with 168 monthly complaints; ELP can use social media only as a supporting channel.

Face-to-face teams can also demonstrate the 96.5% meter-reading accuracy and explain how the new meters cut estimated bills, directly addressing the rise in complaints from 3.8% to 6.1% of customers.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to ELP's metering rollout.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with ELP context and some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of ELP's complaints, accounts and costs, with a justified recommendation explaining why television and social media are rejected.

questions.question_text: ELP's 6.1% billing-complaint rate and skilled-engineer turnover are worsening service. Explain two benefits for ELP of its democratic leadership in addressing these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites the 120 engineers and customer staff to contribute ideas on reducing the 6.1% billing complaints and the 3.4-hour outage duration.Greater involvement raises job satisfaction and ownership, so staff are more likely to suggest practical fixes to the 2.9% network fault rate and to explain problems clearly to customers, helping bring complaints down from 168 a month.

Point 2: Consulting employees about the $1,200,000 smart-meter rollout reduces resistance to change and taps the skills of the 30 engineers still to be trained, easing the skilled turnover problem. When staff feel heard under democratic leadership within the hierarchical structure, morale and retention improve, protecting meter-reading accuracy of 96.5% and the 150,000 units supplied to households and small businesses.

Democratic leadership also helps staff accept the new smart meters: when the 30 engineers still to be trained are consulted about rollout timing, they are more likely to cooperate, protecting the 96.5% accuracy and reducing the 168 monthly complaints that signal weak service.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to ELP and the case data.

questions.question_text: ELP wants to reduce skilled-engineer turnover. Consider formal appraisals or a performance-related bonus. Which should ELP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Formal appraisals: Regular appraisals give each of the 120 engineers feedback, agreed targets and a chance to discuss career development, which can raise motivation and reduce the skilled turnover that is undermining the 3.4-hour outage performance. Appraisals also reveal training needs for the 30 staff not yet trained on smart meters. The disadvantages are the management time required across a large workforce and the risk that appraisals become a paper exercise if managers are not trained to give useful feedback.

Performance-related bonus: A bonus tied to fewer complaints or shorter outages would give engineers a direct financial incentive to improve the 6.1% complaint rate and 2.9% fault rate, and could boost effort quickly. However, it adds to wage costs when the minimum wage rises 6.0%, may encourage a narrow focus on measured targets at the expense of wider service quality, and does not by itself address the career-development reasons engineers leave.

Decision: ELP should choose formal appraisals. They tackle the root causes of turnover by giving feedback, recognising potential and identifying the training needs of 30 engineers, which supports the $1,200,000 rollout and the 96.5% accuracy target. The bonus is rejected because it adds cost during a 6.0% wage rise and may distort priorities; ELP can add a modest quality-related element once appraisals are embedded.

Appraisals should set clear targets linked to the 2.9% network fault rate and the 3.4-hour outages, so engineers see how their work affects customers. Reviews can also identify which of the 30 untrained engineers need smart-meter courses first, protecting the $1,200,000 rollout and the 150,000 units supplied to households and small businesses.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two HR options with little application to ELP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of both options in ELP's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensively evaluates both options against cost, motivation and service quality, with a clear decision and explicit reasons for rejecting the alternative.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how ELP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $1,500,000 ÷ ($85 − $60) = $1,500,000 ÷ $25 = 60,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 60,000 power units a year.
Formula: Labour productivity = Output ÷ Number of workers. Substitution: 150,000 units ÷ 120 workers = 1,250 units per worker. Answer: labour productivity is 1,250 units per employee a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways ELP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Break-even of 60,000 units against 150,000 supplied gives a margin of safety of 90,000 units, showing how much demand can fall before a loss.
2. Labour productivity of 1,250 units per worker lets managers track the impact of the 6.1% billing complaints and 3.4-hour outages on efficient operations.
3. Contribution of $25 a unit helps judge whether the $500,000 bank loan and $700,000 share issue can be serviced before the $1,200,000 programme expands.
4. Monitoring unit costs against 14.2% gas and carbon input inflation helps set prices at the $85 level and protect the 2.7% demand growth.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 60,000 units | (ii) Labour productivity = 1,250 units per employee | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 90,000 units; productivity tracking against 6.1% complaints and 3.4-hour outages; servicing $500,000 of debt; and pricing at $85 under 14.2% input inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ELP's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has ELP's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 30.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 35.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 17.5%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit $1,500,000 ÷ revenue $5,000,000 × 100 = 30.0; 2025 $1,960,000 ÷ $5,600,000 × 100 = 35.0. Operating profit $600,000 ÷ revenue $5,000,000 × 100 = 12.0 in 2024 and $840,000 ÷ $5,600,000 × 100 = 15.0 in 2025. Returns on capital: $600,000 ÷ $4,000,000 × 100 = 15.0 in 2024 and $840,000 ÷ $4,800,000 × 100 = 17.5 in 2025. Cost of sales rose from $3,500,000 to $3,640,000 while revenue grew $600,000, so gross profit increased by $460,000. Interest payable fell from $90,000 to $80,000.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. The gross margin rose from 30.0% to 35.0%, showing better control of generation and supply costs despite 14.2% gas and carbon inflation. The operating margin improved from 12.0% to 15.0%, so more revenue survives the $1,500,000 fixed costs. Returns on capital increased from 15.0% to 17.5%, meaning the $4,800,000 of capital employed is used more effectively, even though a $700,000 share issue enlarged the capital base. The gains are supported by real growth in revenue and gross profit. The risk is that a 6.1% complaint rate and 3.4-hour outages could raise costs and damage the customer base if the rollout is poorly managed.

Conclusion: ELP's financial performance has improved. The gross margin (30.0% to 35.0%), operating margin (12.0% to 15.0%) and returns on capital (15.0% to 17.5%) all rose together, backed by higher revenue and gross profit. ELP should protect the gain by using part of the share issue to cut complaints and outages.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or simple changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates all three ratios for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital and interest, and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ELP of introducing battery storage units as part of its sustainable energy programme.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Battery storage helps ELP manage the 14.2% rise in wholesale gas and carbon permits by storing cheaper off-peak power and reducing reliance on expensive peak generation, protecting the $60 variable cost and the $25 contribution on each of the 150,000 units. It also cuts the 3.4-hour outage duration and supports the green credentials of a $1,200,000 programme funded by a $700,000 share issue.

Disadvantage: The storage units are part of the $1,200,000 outlay, funded alongside a $500,000 bank loan while the base rate rises to 5.5%, so cash flow could be tight if demand grows only 2.7%. Installing and maintaining the units needs engineers trained on the new smart meters, yet 30 of 120 engineers lack training and skilled turnover is rising; until the 2.9% fault rate is addressed, storage may not deliver reliable service.

Storage also lets ELP shift demand away from expensive peak periods, helping hold the $85 price steady while household demand grows only 2.7% and wage costs rise 6.0% across the 120-strong workforce.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to ELP and the case data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.5%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 14.2% rise in wholesale gas and carbon-permit input costs will affect ELP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate (4.75% to 5.5%): If ELP's $500,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $500,000 = $3,750 a year (0.0075 × $500,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $1,500,000 a year and zero on a fixed-rate loan. Because ELP is capital-intensive and also raised $700,000 by share issue, higher rates mainly affect future borrowing and customer demand rather than this year's profit.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $13.50 an hour): With a workforce of 120 in engineering and customer service, this raises the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can be invented; the relevant comparison is productivity, 150,000 units ÷ 120 staff = 1,250 units per employee. If that holds and the 6.1% complaint rate falls, the rise is bearable; if outages and turnover cut productivity, unit labour cost rises and the $25 contribution falls.

Input-cost inflation (14.2% gas and carbon permits): The $60 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound is defensible: if the whole $60 rose 14.2%, that adds 14.2% × $60 = $8.52 a unit; over 150,000 units a year that is about $1,278,000 (150,000 × $8.52). That would cut contribution from $25.00 to about $16.48 on every unit, dwarfing the interest effect, though battery storage and the $85 price give ELP some ability to respond.

Conclusion: The 14.2% rise in wholesale gas and carbon input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to all 150,000 units and directly erodes the $25 contribution that supports the $1,200,000 programme, whereas the interest rise is a bounded $3,750 a year and the wage rise can be absorbed if productivity stays at 1,250 units per employee. ELP should accelerate battery storage to cut exposure.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to ELP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on ELP's costs, revenue or financing in context, using insert figures.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes in ELP's context with a well-justified judgement that input cost inflation has the greatest impact and clear reasons why the other two are smaller.
